newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan, India start final day of talks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan, India start final day of talks.

text.p: Pakistani and Indian negotiators started a crucial third and final day of talks on Sunday within sight of the mountains of disputed Kashmir.

"We are going for a final session that should be a make-or-mar session," Pakistan's foreign ministry secretary Shamshad Ahmad told reporters before entering Governor House, a state guesthouse in the Murree hills north of Islamabad.

The guesthouse is located at Kashmir Point, from which the mountains of the divided Himalayan territory, over which India and Pakistan have fought two of their three wars since independence in 1947, are clearly visible.
Ahmad's Indian counterpart, Salman Haider, said the two sides were working on the machinery of future negotiations.
"We have brought all the nuts and bolts with us," he said. "We will examine them and then put them together. We have started tightening the nuts and bolts. Let's hope for the best."
The top foreign ministry diplomats, each backed by a team of half a dozen colleagues, said on Saturday that they had achieved "forward movement" on their second day of peace talks.
"On the whole there has been a forward movement today," Pakistani foreign ministry spokesman Khalid Salim
Sunday's talks would aim to produce an agreed document that would contain working papers from both sides and set out the mechanism for future talks between the arch-rivals, he added.

Before the last session began, Ahmad sidestepped questions on the outcome. "There is no concept of rigidness or softness in diplomacy," he said. "There are always negative and positive attitudes and both sides have shown positive attitudes."
Haider said: "We have come with a positive approach and we have retained that attitude."
Asked if the two sides had agreed to set up working groups on divisive issues, he said: "Please don't jump the gun."

Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and President Farooq Leghari told the Indian delegation during courtesy calls on Saturday that New Delhi should avoid "negative factors" to make the renewed dialogue a success.

Among what Pakistan calls "negative factors" Leghari and Sharif cited a recent alleged violation of Pakistani air space by an Indian spy plane, alleged deployment of missiles near the border and a border clash in which a Pakistan army officer was killed. India denies the air violation and missile deployment.
An official statement quoted Sharif as calling for India to reduce its forces in the Indian-ruled part of Jammu and Kashmir and to improve the human rights situation there.
"The progress should be uniform on a broad spectrum of Indo-Pakistan issues, including the core issue of Kashmir," Sharif was quoted as saying.

Haider told Sharif that Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral had asked him to assure Islamabad that Delhi "wanted to open a new chapter in the relations between the two countries", according to the Pakistani statement.
The current talks follow an ice-breaking round in late March, which paved the way for the two foreign ministers to meet in April and the two prime ministers to get together in May.
The Delhi meeting of foreign secretaries resumed a dialogue which foundered in 1994 over the issue of Kashmir, two-thirds of which is ruled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
